paragraphs: 8 May. What a lovely day! I have spent the whole morning lying in the grass in front of my house, under the enormous plantain tree that spreads over it, shading and sheltering the whole building. I like this part of the country and love living here because I am bound to it by deep roots—profound and delicate roots that bind a man to the soil where his ancestors were born and died. They bind him to what people think and what they eat, to their customs as well as their food, to local expressions, to the peasants’ distinctive language, to the smell of the soil, of the villages and of the air itself.

I love the house I grew up in. From my windows I can see the Seine flowing beside my garden, on the other side of the road, almost through my grounds—the great, broad Seine that goes to Rouen and Havre, covered with boats travelling back and forth.

Down there to the left lies Rouen, that great town with its blue roofs beneath its pointed Gothic towers. There are countless towers, slender or broad, with the cathedral spire rising above them all. They are full of bells that ring through the blue air on fine mornings, sending me their sweet, distant iron clang. The breeze carries that metallic sound towards me, now stronger, now weaker, as the wind rises or falls.
What a delicious morning it was!
At about eleven o’clock, a long line of boats passed my gate, pulled by a steam tug as small as a fly, which scarcely puffed as it gave off thick smoke.

After two English schooners, whose red flag fluttered towards the sky, came a magnificent Brazilian three-masted ship, perfectly white and wonderfully clean and shining. I saluted it, though I hardly know why, except that the sight of it gave me great pleasure.
12 May. For the last few days I have had a slight feverish attack, and I feel ill—or rather, low-spirited.

Where do these mysterious influences come from, turning our happiness into discouragement and our self-confidence into self-doubt? One might almost say that the air, the invisible air, is full of unknowable Forces whose mysterious presence we must endure. I wake in the best of spirits, with a desire to sing rising in my throat. Why? I go down beside the water, and suddenly, after walking a short distance, I return home miserable, as though some misfortune were waiting for me there. Why? Has a cold shiver passing over my skin disturbed my nerves and lowered my spirits? Have the shapes of the clouds, the colour of the sky, or the ever-changing colours of the objects around me troubled my thoughts as they passed before my eyes? Who can tell? Everything around us, everything we see without looking at it, everything we touch without knowing it, everything we handle without feeling it, everything we encounter without clearly distinguishing it, affects us and our organs swiftly, surprisingly and inexplicably. Through those organs, it affects our ideas and our very hearts.

How profound is the mystery of the Invisible! We cannot fathom it with our wretched senses. Our eyes cannot see what is too small or too large, too near or too far away—neither the inhabitants of a star nor those of a drop of water… Our ears deceive us by turning vibrations of the air into ringing sounds. They are fairies that perform the miracle of changing movement into noise. Through that transformation they give birth to music, making nature’s silent motion musical… Our sense of smell is weaker than a dog’s… Our sense of taste can scarcely distinguish the age of a wine!
Oh! If only we had other organs that could work other miracles for us, how many new things we might discover around us!

16 May. I am ill, definitely! I was so well last month! I am feverish, horribly feverish—or rather, in a state of feverish exhaustion that makes my mind suffer as much as my body. I constantly have that horrible feeling of some danger threatening me, that dread of an approaching misfortune or death. That foreboding is no doubt an attack of some still-unknown illness, germinating in my flesh and blood.

18 May. I have just returned from consulting my doctor, because I could no longer sleep. He found a rapid pulse, dilated pupils and highly strung nerves, but no alarming symptoms. I must have a course of shower-baths and potassium bromide.

25 May. No change! My condition is very peculiar. As evening approaches, an incomprehensible uneasiness seizes me, as though the night concealed some terrible threat against me. I eat dinner quickly and try to read, but cannot understand the words and can scarcely make out the letters. Then I pace my drawing room, weighed down by a confused, irresistible fear—the fear of sleep and the fear of my bed.

At about ten o’clock I go up to my room. As soon as I am inside, I double-lock and bolt the door. I am frightened—of what? Until now I have been frightened of nothing. I open my cupboards and look under my bed. I listen—I listen—to what? How strange that a simple feeling of discomfort, slowed or quickened circulation, perhaps an irritated nerve fibre, a slight congestion, a small disturbance in the delicate, imperfect workings of our living machinery, can turn the most light-hearted man gloomy and make a coward of the bravest! Then I go to bed and wait for sleep as a man might wait for the executioner. I dread its arrival. My heart pounds, my legs tremble, and my whole body shivers beneath the warm bedclothes, until I suddenly fall asleep, as someone might throw himself into a pool of stagnant water to drown. I no longer feel sleep approaching as I once did—this treacherous sleep that is close to me, watching me, about to seize me by the head, close my eyes and annihilate me.

I sleep—a long time, perhaps two or three hours—then a dream—no, a nightmare—takes hold of me. I feel that I am in bed and asleep—I feel it and know it—and I also feel somebody coming close to me, looking at me, touching me, climbing onto my bed, kneeling on my chest, taking my neck in his hands and squeezing it—squeezing with all his strength to strangle me.

I struggle, bound by that terrible helplessness that paralyses us in dreams. I try to cry out, but I cannot. I want to move—I cannot. With the most violent efforts, out of breath, I try to turn over and throw off this being that is crushing and suffocating me—I cannot!

Then, suddenly, I wake, shaking and drenched in sweat. I light a candle and find myself alone. After that crisis, which happens every night, I eventually fall asleep and sleep peacefully until morning.

2 June. My condition has worsened. What is wrong with me? The bromide does me no good, and the shower-baths have no effect at all. Sometimes, to tire myself out, although I am already exhausted enough, I walk in the forest of Roumare. At first I used to think the fresh light and gentle air, steeped in the scent of herbs and leaves, would put new blood in my veins and fresh energy in my heart. I turned onto a broad riding path through the wood, then towards La Bouille along a narrow path between two rows of extremely tall trees. They formed a thick, green, almost black roof between the sky and me.

A sudden shiver ran through me—not a cold shiver, but a shiver of agony. I quickened my steps, uneasy at being alone in the wood, stupidly and unreasonably frightened by its profound solitude. Suddenly I felt as though I were being followed, as though somebody were walking at my heels, close, very close, near enough to touch me.

I turned round suddenly, but I was alone. Behind me I saw nothing except the straight, broad riding path, empty between the tall trees, horribly empty. In the other direction it stretched away into the distance and looked just the same, terrible.

I closed my eyes. Why? Then I began spinning very quickly on one heel, like a top. I nearly fell and opened my eyes. The trees danced around me and the earth heaved; I had to sit down. Then—ah! I could no longer remember which way I had come! What a strange thought! What a strange, strange thought! I had no idea at all. I set off to the right and got back onto the avenue that had led me into the middle of the forest.
3 June. I have had a terrible night. I shall go away for a few weeks. No doubt a journey will restore me.
2 July. I have returned completely cured, and have had a delightful trip into the bargain. I went to Mont Saint-Michel, which I had never seen before.

What a sight, arriving as I did at Avranches towards the end of the day! The town stands on a hill, and I was taken into the public garden at its far edge. I cried out in astonishment. An extraordinarily large bay stretched as far as I could see between two hills that disappeared into the mist. In the middle of that immense yellow bay, beneath a clear, golden sky, a strange hill rose from the sand, dark and pointed. The sun had just disappeared. Beneath the still-flaming sky stood the outline of that fantastic rock, bearing a fantastic monument on its summit.

At daybreak I went to it. The tide was low, as it had been the night before, and I saw that wonderful abbey rising before me as I approached. After several hours’ walking, I reached the enormous mass of rocks supporting the little town, which was dominated by the great church. I climbed the steep, narrow street and entered the most wonderful Gothic building ever built to God on earth. It was as large as a town, full of low rooms that seemed buried beneath vaulted roofs, and lofty galleries supported by delicate columns.

I entered that gigantic granite jewel, as light as a piece of lace, covered with towers and slender belfries reached by spiral staircases. Their strange heads bristled with chimeras, devils, fantastic animals and monstrous flowers. Joined by finely carved arches, they rose into the blue sky by day and the black sky by night.

When I reached the summit, I said to the monk accompanying me, “Father, how happy you must be here!” He replied, “It is very windy, sir.” We began talking as we watched the rising tide sweep over the sand and cover it with a steel breastplate.
Then the monk told me stories, all the old stories of the place—legends, nothing but legends.

One struck me strongly. The country people of the Mornet declare that at night you can hear voices talking in the sand, followed by two goats bleating, one with a strong voice and the other with a weak one. Sceptics say it is nothing but the cries of seabirds, which sometimes sound like bleating and sometimes like human lamentation. But fishermen caught out late swear they have met an old shepherd wandering over the downs between two tides, around that little town so far from the world. They can never see his head, which is covered by his cloak. He leads the way before two goats: a male with a man’s face, and a female with a woman’s face, both white-haired. The goats talk incessantly, quarrelling in a strange language, then suddenly stop talking to bleat with all their strength.

“Do you believe it?” I asked the monk. “I hardly know,” he replied. I continued, “If there are beings besides ourselves on this earth, how can we have gone so long without knowing it? Why haven’t you seen them? Why haven’t I seen them?” He replied, “Do we see even a hundred-thousandth of what exists? Look at the wind, the strongest force in nature. It knocks men down, blows down buildings, uproots trees, raises the sea into mountains of water, destroys cliffs and casts great ships onto the breakers. The wind kills, whistles, sighs and roars—have you ever seen it? Can you see it? Yet it exists all the same.”
That simple reasoning silenced me. The man was a philosopher, or perhaps a fool; I could not say exactly which, so I held my tongue. What he had said had often been in my own thoughts.

3 July. I have slept badly. Certainly some feverish influence is at work here, for my coachman is suffering in the same way as I am. When I returned home yesterday, I noticed his unusual paleness and asked, “What is wrong with you, Jean?” “The trouble is that I never get any rest, and my nights devour my days. Since you went away, sir, there has been a spell over me.”
The other servants are all well, however, but I am very frightened of having another attack myself.

4 July. It has definitely taken hold of me again, for my old nightmares have returned. Last night I felt somebody leaning on me, sucking my life from between my lips with his mouth. Yes, he was sucking it out of my neck like a leech. Then he got up, satisfied, and I woke so beaten, crushed and annihilated that I could not move. If this continues for a few days, I shall certainly go away again.
5 July. Have I lost my reason? What happened, what I saw last night, is so strange that my mind reels when I think of it!
As I now do every evening, I had locked my door. Then, feeling thirsty, I drank half a glass of water and happened to notice that the water bottle was full right up to its cut-glass stopper.
I went to bed and fell into one of my terrible sleeps, from which an even more terrible shock woke me about two hours later.

Imagine a sleeping man being murdered, waking with a knife in his chest, a rattle in his throat, covered in blood, unable to breathe, about to die and understanding none of it—that was what it was like.

When I recovered my senses, I was thirsty again. I lit a candle and went to the table where my water bottle stood. I picked it up and tilted it over my glass, but nothing came out. It was empty! It was completely empty! At first I could not understand it at all. Then suddenly such a terrible feeling seized me that I had to sit down—or rather, fell into a chair! I sprang up to look around me, then sat down again in front of the transparent crystal bottle, overcome with astonishment and fear! I stared at it, trying to work out what had happened, and my hands shook! Somebody had drunk the water—but who? Me? Me, without a doubt. Surely it could only have been me? In that case I was a sleepwalker. Without knowing it, I lived that mysterious double life that makes us wonder whether there are two beings inside us. Or whether, at such moments, when our soul lies dormant, some strange, unknowable, invisible being animates our captive body, which obeys that other being as it obeys us, and even more than it obeys us.

Oh! Who will understand my horrible agony? Who will understand what a man feels when he is sane, wide awake and full of good sense, yet looks in horror through the glass of a water bottle at what remains of a little water that vanished while he slept? I stayed there until daylight, not daring to go back to bed.
6 July. I am going mad. Once again, everything in my water bottle was drunk during the night—or rather, I drank it!
But was it me? Was it me? Who could it have been? Who? Oh, God! Am I going mad? Who will save me?
10 July. I have just been through some astonishing ordeals. I am definitely mad! And yet!—

On 6 July, before going to bed, I put wine, milk, water, bread and strawberries on my table. Somebody drank—I drank—all the water and a little milk, but the wine, bread and strawberries were untouched.
On 7 July I repeated the experiment with the same results. On 8 July I left out the water and milk, and nothing was touched.

Finally, on 9 July I put only water and milk on my table, carefully wrapping the bottles in white muslin and tying down their stoppers. Then I rubbed my lips, beard and hands with pencil lead and went to bed.

Irresistible sleep seized me, soon followed by a terrible awakening. I had not moved, and there were no marks on my sheets. I rushed to the table. The muslin around the bottles was intact. Trembling with fear, I untied the string. All the water had been drunk, and so had the milk! Ah! Great God!—
I must leave for Paris immediately.

12 July. Paris. I must have lost my head these last few days! I must be the plaything of my exhausted imagination—unless I really am a sleepwalker, or have fallen under one of those influences whose existence has been proved but which remain unexplained, the influences called suggestions. In any case, my mental state bordered on madness, and twenty-four hours in Paris were enough to restore my balance.

Yesterday, after doing some business and paying visits that breathed fresh, invigorating air into my mind, I ended the evening at the Théâtre Français. They were performing a play by Alexandre Dumas the Younger, and his active, powerful mind completed my cure. Certainly solitude is dangerous for active minds. We need people around us who can think and talk. When we are alone for a long time, we fill the space around us with phantoms.

I returned to my hotel along the boulevards in excellent spirits. Jostled by the crowd, I thought with some irony of the previous week’s terrors and suspicions, because I had believed—yes, I had believed—that an invisible being lived under my roof. How weak our minds are, and how quickly they become terrified and lose their way when some small, incomprehensible fact strikes us.
Instead of simply concluding, “I do not understand because the cause escapes me,” we immediately imagine terrible mysteries and supernatural powers.

14 July. Festival of the Republic. I walked through the streets, and the firecrackers and flags amused me like a child. Yet how foolish to be merry on a fixed date by government decree. The populace is an idiotic flock of sheep, patient and steady one moment, in ferocious revolt the next. Tell it, “Enjoy yourself,” and it enjoys itself. Tell it, “Go and fight your neighbour,” and it goes and fights. Tell it, “Vote for the Emperor,” and it votes for the Emperor. Then tell it, “Vote for the Republic,” and it votes for the Republic.

Those who lead it are stupid too. But instead of obeying people, they obey principles, which can only be stupid, sterile and false precisely because they are principles: ideas held to be certain and unchangeable, in a world where nothing is certain, since light is an illusion and sound is an illusion.
16 July. Yesterday I saw things that troubled me deeply.

I was dining at the home of my cousin, Mrs Sablé, whose husband is colonel of the 76th Chasseurs at Limoges. Two young women were there, one of whom was married to a physician, Dr. Parent. He devotes much of his work to nervous diseases and to the extraordinary phenomena now arising from experiments in hypnotism and suggestion.

He spoke at length about the tremendous results achieved by English scientists and the doctors of the medical school at Nancy. The facts he presented seemed so strange that I declared I did not believe them at all.

“We are,” he declared, “about to discover one of nature’s most important secrets. I mean one of its most important secrets on this earth, for certainly there are secrets of a different order of importance up there among the stars. Ever since man began to think, ever since he could express and write down his thoughts, he has felt close to a mystery that his crude, imperfect senses cannot penetrate. He tries to make up for the limited powers of his organs through the efforts of his intellect. While that intellect was still in its earliest stage, this contact with invisible spirits took commonplace, though terrifying, forms. From that came popular belief in the supernatural, legends of wandering spirits, fairies, gnomes and ghosts. I might even say the legend of God, for our ideas of the creator as a craftsman, whatever religion has handed them down to us, are certainly the most mediocre, stupidest and most unacceptable inventions ever to spring from the frightened brains of human beings. Nothing is truer than Voltaire’s saying: ‘God made man in His own image, but man has certainly returned the favour.’

“But for a little more than a century, people seem to have sensed something new approaching. Mesmer and others put us on an unexpected track, and especially in the last two or three years, we have achieved truly surprising results.”
My cousin, who is also very sceptical, smiled. Dr. Parent asked her, “Would you like me to try to put you to sleep, madam?” “Yes, certainly.”

She sat in an armchair, and he began staring fixedly at her to mesmerise her. I suddenly felt rather uneasy, my heart beating hard and my throat tightening. I saw Mrs Sablé’s eyes growing heavy, her mouth twitching and her chest heaving. After ten minutes, she was asleep.

“Stand behind her,” the doctor told me, so I took a seat behind her. He placed a visiting card in her hands and said, “This is a mirror. What do you see in it?” She replied, “I see my cousin.” “What is he doing?” “He is twisting his moustache.” “And now?” “He is taking a photograph out of his pocket.” “Whose photograph is it?” “His own.”
That was true, and the photograph had been given to me that same evening at the hotel.
“How is he posed in the portrait?” “He is standing with his hat in his hand.”
So she saw images on that card, on that piece of white cardboard, as though she were seeing them in a mirror.
The young women were frightened and exclaimed, “That is quite enough! Quite, quite enough!”

But the doctor told her firmly, “Tomorrow morning you will get up at eight o’clock. Then you will visit your cousin at his hotel and ask him to lend you five thousand francs, which your husband demands from you and will ask for when he sets out on his coming journey.”
Then he woke her.

Returning to my hotel, I thought over that strange session and was assailed by doubts. I did not doubt my cousin’s absolute, unquestionable honesty: I had known her ever since she was a child, as well as if she were my own sister. But might the doctor have played a trick? Perhaps he had hidden a mirror in his hand and shown it to the sleeping young woman at the same time as the card? Professional magicians do things just as strange.
So I went home and to bed. This morning, at about half past eight, my footman woke me, saying, “Mrs Sablé has asked to see you immediately, sir.” I dressed hurriedly and went to her.

She sat down in some agitation, her eyes on the floor, and spoke without lifting her veil. “My dear cousin, I am going to ask you a great favour.” “What is it, cousin?” “I do not like to tell you, but I must. I absolutely need five thousand francs.” “What—you?” “Yes, me—or rather, my husband, who has asked me to get the money for him.”

I was so astonished that I stammered my answers. I wondered whether she and Dr. Parent had really been making fun of me, whether it was simply a very well-acted farce arranged in advance. But when I looked closely at her, my doubts vanished. She was trembling with distress, so painful was it for her to take this step, and I was sure sobs were caught in her throat.
I knew she was very rich, so I continued, “What! Doesn’t your husband have five thousand francs available? Come, think. Are you sure he asked you to get them from me?”
She hesitated for a few seconds, as though struggling to search her memory, then answered, “Yes… yes, I am quite sure.” “Has he written to you?”

She hesitated again and thought, and I could imagine the torment in her mind. She did not know. She knew only that she was to borrow five thousand francs from me for her husband. So she lied. “Yes, he has written to me.” “When, may I ask? You said nothing about it yesterday.” “I received his letter this morning.” “Can you show it to me?” “No, no… no… it contained private matters… things too personal to us… I burnt it.” “So your husband gets into debt?”
She hesitated again, then murmured, “I do not know.” I said bluntly, “I do not have five thousand francs available at the moment, my dear cousin.”
She gave a kind of cry, as though in pain. “Oh! Oh! I beg you, I beg you to get them for me…”
She grew agitated and clasped her hands as though praying to me! I heard the tone of her voice change. She wept and stammered, tormented and ruled by the irresistible command she had received.
“Oh! Oh! I beg you to… if you knew what I am suffering… I need them today.”
I pitied her. “You shall have them later, I swear to you.” “Oh! Thank you! Thank you! How kind you are!”

I continued, “Do you remember what happened at your house last night?” “Yes.” “Do you remember Dr. Parent putting you to sleep?” “Yes.” “Well then, he ordered you to come to me this morning and borrow five thousand francs. At this moment, you are obeying that suggestion.”
She thought for a few moments, then replied:
“But since it is my husband who wants them…”

For a whole hour I tried to convince her, without success. When she had gone, I went to the doctor. He was just going out. He listened with a smile and said, “Do you believe now?” “Yes, I cannot help it.” “Let us go to your cousin’s.”

She was already dozing on a couch, overcome with exhaustion. The doctor felt her pulse and looked at her for some time, holding one hand towards her eyes. They gradually closed under the irresistible power of that magnetic influence. When she was asleep, he said:
“Your husband no longer needs the five thousand francs! You must therefore forget that you asked your cousin to lend them to you. If he speaks of it, you will not understand him.”

He woke her. I took out a wallet and said, “Here is what you asked me for this morning, my dear cousin.” But she was so surprised that I did not dare insist. Nevertheless, I tried to remind her of what had happened. She denied it vigorously, thought I was making fun of her, and finally came very close to losing her temper.
There! I have just returned, and have been unable to eat any lunch, for the experiment has completely upset me.
19 July. Many people I have told about this experience have laughed at me. I no longer know what to think. The wise man says, “Perhaps?”

21 July. I dined at Bougival, then spent the evening at a boatmen’s ball. Everything certainly depends on place and surroundings. It would be utterly foolish to believe in the supernatural on the île de la Grenouillière… but on the summit of Mont Saint-Michel?… and in India? Our surroundings have a terrible influence over us. I shall return home next week.
30 July. I returned to my own house yesterday. Everything is going well.
2 August. Nothing new. The weather is splendid, and I spend my days watching the Seine flow past.

4 August. Quarrels among my servants. They say glasses are being broken in the cupboards at night. The footman accuses the cook, who accuses the seamstress, who accuses the other two. Who is the culprit? It would take someone clever to tell.
6 August. This time I am not mad. I have seen… I have seen… I have seen!… I can doubt no longer… I have seen it!…

At two o’clock I was walking among my rose trees in full sunlight… along the path bordered by autumn roses that are beginning to fall. I stopped to look at a Géant de Bataille with three splendid blooms. Close beside me, I distinctly saw the stem of one rose bend as though an invisible hand had bent it, then break as though that hand had picked it! The flower rose, tracing the curve a hand would follow in lifting it towards a mouth. It remained suspended in the transparent air, alone and motionless, a terrible red spot three yards from my eyes. Desperately I rushed to seize it! I found nothing: it had disappeared. Then furious anger at myself seized me, for a reasonable, serious man cannot be allowed to have such hallucinations.

But was it a hallucination? I turned to look for the stalk and immediately found it under the bush, freshly broken, between two other roses still on the branch. I returned home deeply disturbed. For now I am certain, as certain as I am that day and night alternate, that an invisible being exists close to me. It lives on milk and water, can touch objects, take them and move them, and must therefore have a material nature, although our senses cannot perceive it. And it lives, as I do, beneath my roof…
7 August. I slept peacefully. He drank the water from my decanter but did not disturb my sleep.

I ask myself whether I am mad. As I was walking beside the river in the sunshine just now, doubts about my sanity arose—not vague doubts like those I have had before, but precise and absolute ones. I have seen mad people, and known some who were intelligent, lucid, even clear-sighted in every concern of life except one. They spoke clearly, readily and profoundly about everything. Then suddenly their thoughts struck the breakers of their madness and shattered there, scattering and sinking into that furious, terrible sea of bounding waves, fogs and squalls that we call madness.

I would certainly think I was mad, utterly mad, if I were not conscious of my condition, if I did not know it perfectly, if I could not understand it by analysing it with complete clarity. I would, in fact, be a rational man suffering from a hallucination. Some unknown disturbance must have arisen in my brain, one of those disturbances that physiologists today try to observe and pinpoint. It must have opened a deep gulf in my mind and in the order and logic of my ideas. Similar things happen in dreams, which lead us through the most improbable successions of visions without surprising us. Our machinery for checking things and our sense of control have gone to sleep, while our imagination remains awake and working. Could one of the imperceptible keys on my brain’s keyboard have been paralysed? After an accident, some people lose their memory for proper names, verbs, numbers or merely dates. It has now been proved that every part of thought has its own location. Why, then, should it be surprising if my ability to recognise the unreality of certain hallucinations has been destroyed for a time?

I thought about all this as I walked beside the water. The sun shone brightly on the river and made the earth delightful. It filled my gaze with love for life, for the swallows whose agility always delights my eyes, for the riverside plants whose rustling pleases my ears.

Gradually, however, an inexplicable discomfort seized me. Some unknown force seemed to be numbing and stopping me, preventing me from going further and calling me back. I felt that painful urge to return that weighs on you when you have left a loved one ill at home and are seized by a foreboding that their condition has worsened.
So I returned against my will, certain that bad news awaited me—a letter or a telegram. There was nothing. I was more surprised and uneasy than I would have been by another fantastic vision.

8 August. I spent a terrible evening yesterday. He no longer shows himself, but I feel him near me, watching me, looking at me, penetrating me, dominating me. He is more fearsome when he hides like this than if he made his constant, invisible presence known through supernatural phenomena. Nevertheless, I slept.
9 August. Nothing, but I am afraid.
10 August. Nothing. What will happen tomorrow?
11 August. Still nothing. I cannot stay at home with this fear hanging over me and these thoughts in my mind. I shall go away.

12 August. Ten o’clock at night. All day I have tried to leave and have been unable to. I wanted to perform this simple, easy act of freedom—go out, get into my carriage to go to Rouen—and I have been unable to do it. Why?

13 August. When certain illnesses attack us, every spring in our physical machinery seems broken, all our energy destroyed, all our muscles slack. Our bones seem as soft as our flesh, our blood as liquid as water. In a strange and distressing way, I am experiencing this in my inner self. I no longer have any strength, courage or self-control, or even the power to set my own will in motion. I can no longer will anything. Someone else does it for me, and I obey.

14 August. I am lost! Somebody possesses my soul and rules it! Somebody commands all my actions, all my movements, all my thoughts. I am nothing in myself any more, nothing but an enslaved, terrified spectator of everything I do. I want to go out; I cannot. He does not want to, so I remain trembling and distraught in the armchair where he keeps me sitting. I only want to get up and rouse myself, so that I can think I am still my own master. I cannot! I am riveted to my chair, and my chair sticks to the ground so firmly that no force could move us.

Then suddenly I must, I must go to the bottom of my garden, pick strawberries and eat them. And I go. I pick the strawberries and eat them! Oh, my God! My God! Is there a God? If there is, free me! Save me! Help me! Forgiveness! Pity! Mercy! Save me! Oh, what suffering! What torture! What horror!

15 August. This is certainly how my poor cousin was possessed and controlled when she came to borrow five thousand francs from me. She was under the power of a strange will that had entered her like another soul, like another parasitic, ruling soul. Is the world coming to an end?
But who is he, this invisible being who rules me? This unknowable being, this wanderer from a supernatural race?

So invisible beings exist! Why, then, since the beginning of the world, have they never revealed themselves in exactly the way they have to me? I have never read anything resembling what happens in my house. Oh, if only I could leave it, if only I could go away and flee, never to return, I would be saved. But I cannot.

16 August. Today I managed to escape for two hours, like a prisoner finding his dungeon door accidentally open. Suddenly I felt free and felt that he was far away. I ordered the horses to be harnessed as quickly as possible and drove to Rouen. Oh, how delightful to be able to say to a man who obeyed you, “Go to Rouen!”
I made him stop outside the library and begged them to lend me Dr. Herrmann Herestauss’s treatise on the unknown inhabitants of the ancient and modern world.

As I was getting into my carriage, I meant to say, “To the railway station!” Instead I shouted—I did not say it, I shouted—so loudly that all the passers-by turned round, “Home!” I fell back onto the carriage cushion, overcome by mental agony. He had found me and regained possession of me.

17 August. Oh, what a night! What a night! And yet it seems I ought to rejoice. I read until one in the morning! Herestauss, Doctor of Philosophy and Theogony, wrote about the history and manifestations of all those invisible beings that hover around man, or of which he dreams. He describes their origins, their domains, their powers, but none resembles the one that haunts me. One might say that, ever since man began to think, he has sensed and feared a new being, stronger than himself, his successor in this world. Perhaps, feeling that being near but unable to predict the nature of that master, he has invented, in his terror, the whole race of hidden beings, vague phantoms born of fear.

After reading until one in the morning, I went to sit at the open window, to cool my forehead and my thoughts in the calm night air. It was so pleasant and warm! How I would once have enjoyed a night like that!

There was no moon, but the stars sent their rays through the dark heavens. Who lives in those worlds? What forms, what living beings, what animals are there? What do the thinkers in those distant worlds know that we do not? What can they do that we cannot? What do they see that is unknown to us? Will one of them someday cross space and appear on our earth to conquer it, just as the Norsemen once crossed the sea to subdue nations weaker than themselves?
We are so weak, so unarmed, so ignorant, so small—we who live on this particle of mud spinning in a drop of water.

Thinking like this in the cool night air, I fell asleep. After about three-quarters of an hour, I opened my eyes without moving, woken by some confused, strange sensation I could not identify. At first I saw nothing. Then suddenly a page of a book left open on my table seemed to turn of its own accord. Not a breath of air had come through my window. Surprised, I waited. About four minutes later I saw, I saw, yes, I saw with my own eyes another page rise and fall onto the others, as though a finger had turned it. My armchair was empty—appeared empty—but I knew he was there, he, sitting in my place and reading. With a furious leap, the leap of an enraged wild beast intent on disembowelling its tamer, I crossed the room to seize him, strangle him, kill him!… But before I could reach it, my chair fell over as though somebody had fled from me… my table rocked, my lamp fell and went out, and my window closed as though a thief had been surprised and escaped into the night, shutting it behind him.
So he had fled. He had been afraid—he, afraid of me!
So… so… tomorrow… or later… some day… I should be able to hold him in my grasp and crush him against the ground! Don’t dogs sometimes bite and strangle their masters?
18 August. I have thought all day long. Oh, yes, I shall obey him, follow his impulses, fulfil all his wishes, show myself humble, submissive, a coward. He is stronger, but the hour will come…

19 August. I know… I know… I know everything! I have just read this in the Revue du Monde Scientifique: “Curious news reaches us from Rio de Janeiro. Madness—an epidemic of madness comparable to the contagious madness that struck the people of Europe in the Middle Ages—is now raging in the Province of San-Paulo. The frightened inhabitants are leaving their houses, deserting their villages and abandoning their land. They say they are pursued, possessed and ruled like human cattle by invisible but tangible beings, a species of vampire that feeds on their life while they sleep. These beings also drink water and milk, apparently touching no other nourishment.

“Professor Dom Pedro Henriques, accompanied by several medical scientists, has gone to the Province of San-Paulo to study the origins and manifestations of this astonishing madness on the spot. He will propose to the Emperor whatever measures seem to him best suited to restoring the mad population to reason.”

Ah! Ah! Now I remember that fine Brazilian three-masted ship that passed my windows on its way up the Seine on 8 May! I thought it so pretty, so white and bright! That Being was aboard her, coming from the place where its race originated. And it saw me! It saw my house, which was white too, and sprang from the ship onto the land. Oh, good heavens!

Now I know; I can sense the truth. The reign of man is over, and he has come. He is the one whom troubled priests exorcised, whom sorcerers summoned on dark nights without yet seeing him appear. In their forebodings, the world’s temporary masters gave him all the monstrous or graceful forms of gnomes, spirits, genies, fairies and familiar spirits. After those crude conceptions born of primitive fear, more clear-sighted men foresaw him more clearly. Mesmer sensed him. Ten years ago, physicians discovered the precise nature of his power, even before he used it himself. They played with that weapon of their new Lord: the rule of a mysterious will over an enslaved human soul. They called it magnetism, hypnotism, suggestion… what do I know? I have seen them amusing themselves like impudent children with this horrible power! Woe to us! Woe to man! He has come, the… the… what does he call himself… the… I think he is shouting his name to me and I cannot hear him… the… yes… he is shouting it… I am listening… I cannot… repeat… it… Horla… I have heard… the Horla… it is he… the Horla… he has come!…

Ah! The vulture has eaten the pigeon, the wolf has eaten the lamb, the lion has devoured the sharp-horned buffalo. Man has killed the lion with an arrow, with a sword, with gunpowder. But the Horla, through the sheer power of his will, will make man what we have made the horse and the ox: his property, his slave and his food. Woe to us!

Yet the animal sometimes rebels and kills the man who has subdued it… I should also like to… I shall be able to… but I must know him, touch him, see him! Scientists say that animals’ eyes, being different from ours, do not see as ours do… And my eye cannot distinguish this newcomer who oppresses me.

Why? Oh! Now I remember the monk’s words at Mont Saint-Michel: “Can we see even a hundred-thousandth of what exists? Look at the wind, the strongest force in nature. It knocks men down, blows down buildings, uproots trees, raises the sea into mountains of water, destroys cliffs and casts great ships onto the breakers. The wind kills, whistles, sighs and roars—have you ever seen it? Can you see it? Yet it exists all the same!”

I went on thinking: my eyes are so weak, so imperfect, that they cannot even distinguish solid objects as transparent as glass!… If a sheet of glass without tin foil behind it blocked my path, I would run into it, just as a bird that has flown into a room smashes its head against the windowpanes. Besides, a thousand things deceive my sight and lead it astray. Why should it be surprising, then, that it cannot perceive a new body through which light passes?

A new being! Why not? It was surely bound to come! Why should we be the last? We cannot see it as we see the other beings created before us. That is because its nature is more perfect, its body finer and more fully developed than ours. Our body is so weak, so awkwardly designed, burdened with organs that are always tired and always under strain, like overcomplicated locks. It lives like a plant and a beast, struggling to nourish itself on air, plants and flesh. It is an animal machine, prey to illness, malformation and decay: short of breath, badly regulated, simple and strange, ingeniously ill-made, both crude and delicate—a mere outline of a being that might become intelligent and great.

There are only a few of us, so few in this world, from the oyster up to man. Why should there not be one more, once the interval separating the successive appearances of all the different species has passed?

Why not one more? Why not other trees, too, with immense, splendid flowers scenting whole regions? Why not other elements besides fire, air, earth and water? There are four, only four, those fathers that nourish the different beings! What a pity! Why not forty, four hundred, four thousand? How poor everything is, how paltry and wretched! Given so grudgingly, imagined so dryly, made so clumsily! Ah, the elephant and the hippopotamus—what grace! And the camel—what elegance!

But the butterfly, you will say—a flying flower! I dream of one as large as a hundred worlds, with wings whose shape, beauty, colours and movement I cannot even express. But I see it… it flutters from star to star, refreshing them and perfuming them with the gentle, harmonious breath of its flight!… And the people up there watch it pass in an ecstasy of delight!…
What is wrong with me? It is he, the Horla, who haunts me and makes me think these foolish things! He is inside me, becoming my soul. I shall kill him!

19 August. I shall kill him. I have seen him! Yesterday I sat at my table and pretended to write very busily. I knew he would come prowling around me, close, so close that perhaps I could touch him, seize him. And then!… Then I would have the strength of desperation. I would have my hands, my knees, my chest, my forehead, my teeth to strangle him, crush him, bite him, tear him to pieces. I watched for him with every overexcited organ of my body.
I had lit my two lamps and the eight wax candles on my mantelpiece, as though that light could reveal him.

Opposite me stood my bed, my old oak bed with its columns. On my right was the fireplace; on my left, the door, carefully closed after I had left it open for a while to lure him in. Behind me was a very tall wardrobe with a mirror in it, which I used for my daily grooming and in which I habitually looked at myself from head to foot whenever I passed.
I pretended to write to deceive him, for he too was watching me. Suddenly I felt—I was certain—that he was reading over my shoulder, that he was there, almost touching my ear.

I rose so quickly, my hands outstretched, that I nearly fell. Well?… It was as bright as midday, but I could not see myself in the mirror!… It was empty, clear, deep, full of light! But my figure was not reflected there… and I, I was standing opposite it! I saw the large, clear mirror from top to bottom and stared with unsteady eyes. I dared not advance, dared not move, although I felt perfectly that he was there and yet would escape me again—he whose imperceptible body had absorbed my reflection.

How frightened I was! Then suddenly I began to see myself through a mist in the depths of the mirror, a mist like a sheet of water. That water seemed to flow slowly from left to right, making my figure clearer every moment. It was like the end of an eclipse. Whatever hid me seemed to have no distinct outline, only a sort of opaque transparency that gradually became clearer.
At last I could distinguish myself completely, as I do every day when I look at myself.
I had seen it! The horror stayed with me and makes me shudder even now.

20 August. How could I kill it if I could not get hold of it? Poison? But it would see me mixing it into the water. And would our poisons affect its intangible body? No… no… no doubt about it… Then?… Then?…

21 August. I sent for a blacksmith from Rouen and ordered iron shutters for my room, like those fitted to the ground floors of some private residences in Paris against thieves. He will make a similar door as well. I have made myself look like a coward, but I do not care!…
10 September. Rouen, Hotel Continental. It is done… it is done… but is he dead? What I have seen has completely unsettled my mind.
Well, yesterday, after the locksmith had fitted the iron shutters and door, I left everything open until midnight, although it was growing cold.

Suddenly I felt he was there, and joy, mad joy, possessed me. I rose quietly and walked to the right and left for a while, so that he would suspect nothing. Then I casually took off my boots and put on my slippers. I fastened the iron shutters, hurried back to the door and double-locked it with a padlock, putting the key in my pocket.

Suddenly I noticed him moving restlessly around me. He, in his turn, was frightened and ordering me to let him out. I almost gave in, though I had not yet done so. With my back to the door, I half opened it, just enough to let myself out backwards. I am very tall, and my head touched the lintel. I was sure he had been unable to escape. I shut him in quite alone, quite alone. What happiness! I had him trapped. Then I ran downstairs. In the drawing room beneath my bedroom, I took the two lamps and poured all their oil onto the carpet, the furniture, everywhere. I set fire to it and escaped, after carefully double-locking the door.

I hid in a clump of laurel bushes at the bottom of the garden. How long it was! How long it was! Everything was dark, silent, motionless. Not a breath of air, not a star—only heavy banks of clouds I could not see, but which weighed, oh, so heavily on my soul.

I watched my house and waited. How long it was! I was beginning to think the fire had gone out by itself, or that he had put it out, when one of the lower windows gave way under the violence of the flames. A long, soft, caressing sheet of red flame climbed the white wall and kissed it as high as the roof. Light fell on the trees, branches and leaves, and they too shivered with fear! Birds awoke, a dog began to howl, and it seemed to me that day was breaking! Almost immediately, two more windows shattered. I saw that the entire lower part of my house was a terrible furnace. But a cry—a horrible, shrill, heartrending cry, a woman’s cry—rang through the night, and two attic windows opened! I had forgotten the servants! I saw their terror-stricken faces and frantically waving arms!…
Overwhelmed with horror, I set off running towards the village, shouting, “Help! Help! Fire! Fire!” I met people already coming to the scene and went back with them to see!

By then the house was nothing but a horrible, magnificent funeral pyre, a monstrous funeral pyre lighting up the whole countryside, a funeral pyre where people were burning and he was burning too—He, He, my prisoner, that new Being, the new master, the Horla!

Suddenly the whole roof collapsed between the walls, and a volcano of flames shot into the sky. Through every window opening onto that furnace, I saw flames darting, and I thought he was there in that kiln, dead.
Dead? Perhaps?… His body? Wasn’t his transparent body immune to the things that would kill ours?

What if he was not dead?… Perhaps only time has power over that Invisible and Terrifying Being. Why have this transparent, unrecognisable body, this body belonging to a spirit, if it too must fear illness, infirmity and premature destruction?

Premature destruction? All human terror springs from that! After man, the Horla. After the one who could die any day, at any hour, at any moment, through any accident, came the one who would die only at his own appointed hour and minute, because he had reached the limits of his existence!
No… no… without any doubt… he is not dead. Then… then… I suppose I must kill myself!
